title: Major scale and intervals
summary: The major scale formula, scale degrees, movable fingerings, and naming and hearing intervals.

lessons.title: The major scale formula
lessons.summary: Build the major scale from whole and half steps, see it on one string, and play C major in open position.

steps.title: A pattern of steps
steps.body:
A **scale** is a set of notes in order, starting and ending on a home note called the **tonic**.

The **major scale** is the reference point for almost all music theory. It always uses the same pattern of steps:

**W – W – H – W – W – W – H**

(W = whole step = 2 frets, H = half step = 1 fret.)

From C: C –W– D –W– E –H– F –W– G –W– A –W– B –H– C. The half steps land exactly on E–F and B–C, so **C major has no sharps or flats**.

steps.title: The formula on one string
steps.body:
Playing a scale along one string shows the pattern as distances. Start on the open low E and follow W W H W W W H:

Frets **0 – 2 – 4 – 5 – 7 – 9 – 11 – 12**

That spells **E F# G# A B C# D# E**. Every letter appears once, in order, and four of them need sharps to fit the pattern. This is why keys have sharps or flats: the formula decides them, not the letters.

steps.title: E major on one string
steps.caption: Up and down string 6. Listen for the two half steps near the top of each half.

exercise.prompt: Play E major along the low E string: frets 0 2 4 5 7 9 11 12, then back down.

mistakeTips: Say "whole, whole, half" as you move: two frets, two frets, one fret.
The half steps are frets 4→5 and 11→12.

steps.title: C major in open position
steps.body:
Across the strings, the same scale fits in a small area near the nut:

- String 5: **C** (3)
- String 4: **D** (0), **E** (2), **F** (3)
- String 3: **G** (0), **A** (2)
- String 2: **B** (0), **C** (1)

Use finger 1 for fret 1, finger 2 for fret 2, finger 3 for fret 3.

exercise.prompt: Play C major up and down in open position, one note per beat.

mistakeTips: Use alternate picking: down, up, down, up.
Keep fingers hovering close to the strings when not pressing.
The low C is on string 5, fret 3, not the open low E.

questions.prompt: What is the step pattern of the major scale?
choices: W W H W W W H
W H W W H W W
W W W H W W H
questions.explanation: Whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half.

questions.prompt: Why does C major have no sharps or flats?
choices: Its half steps fall on E–F and B–C
questions.explanation: The formula's half steps (3–4 and 7–8) match the natural half steps E–F and B–C.

questions.prompt: What is the third note of E major?
questions.explanation: E –W– F# –W– G#.

questions.prompt: Between which scale degrees are the half steps?
questions.explanation: W W H: the first half step is 3–4. W W W H: the second is 7–8.

reviewItems.answer: W W H W W W H

reviewItems.prompt: Where are the half steps in a major scale?

lessons.title: Scale degrees and G major
lessons.summary: Number and name the scale degrees, play G major over two octaves, and learn a movable fingering.

steps.title: Scale degrees
steps.body:
Each note of a scale has a number, its **scale degree**, counted from the tonic. Theory uses these numbers so ideas work in every key.

| Degree | Name | In C | In G |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | tonic | C | G |
| 2 | supertonic | D | A |
| 3 | mediant | E | B |
| 4 | subdominant | F | C |
| 5 | dominant | G | D |
| 6 | submediant | A | E |
| 7 | leading tone | B | F# |

Degree 7 is the **leading tone**: a half step below the tonic, it sounds like it wants to rise to it. Degree 5, the **dominant**, is the second most important note after the tonic.

steps.title: G major
steps.body:
Apply W W H W W W H from G: **G A B C D E F# G**. The formula needs F# between E and G: E to F# is a whole step, F# to G is a half step. G major has **one sharp**.

Two octaves fit in open position, from the low G on string 6, fret 3 up to the G on string 1, fret 3.

diagram.caption: G major, two octaves, with scale degrees.

exercise.prompt: G major, two octaves, open position. Alternate picking, one note per beat.

mistakeTips: F# appears twice: string 4 fret 4 and string 1 fret 2. Use finger 4 for the first one.
Start the low G with finger 3 so fingers 1–2 are ready for frets 1 and 2 later.
Strict down-up picking even when crossing strings. It feels odd at first and pays off later.

steps.title: A movable fingering
steps.body:
Open-position scales use open strings, so they only work in one key. A fingering with **no open strings** can slide to any fret.

Here is G major in **second position**: the index finger covers fret 2, and each finger covers its own fret (**one finger per fret**: 1 on fret 2, 2 on 3, 3 on 4, 4 on 5). The root is on string 6, fret 3, under finger 2.

Slide the whole fingering up two frets and the root becomes A: you are playing **A major**. The pattern is the same; only the starting fret changes.

diagram.caption: G major, movable fingering. Root under finger 2.

exercise.prompt: Move the fingering up two frets and play A major, one octave, from string 6 fret 5 to string 4 fret 7.

mistakeTips: Index finger at fret 4, finger 2 on the root at fret 5.
Same finger pattern as G: only the position changed.
Say the degrees as you play: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 1.

questions.prompt: What is scale degree 5 of G major?
questions.explanation: G A B C D: D is the fifth note.

questions.prompt: What is the leading tone of G major?
questions.explanation: Degree 7 is a half step below G: F#.

questions.prompt: What is scale degree 4 called?
questions.explanation: 4 = subdominant, 5 = dominant.

questions.prompt: How many sharps are in G major?
questions.explanation: Only F#.

reviewItems.answer: G A B C D E F# G

lessons.title: Intervals: measuring distance
lessons.summary: Name intervals by number and quality, count their half steps, and find them on the fretboard.

steps.title: Interval number
steps.body:
An **interval** is the distance between two notes. Its name has two parts.

The **interval number** counts letter names from the lower note to the upper note, **including both**:

- C to D: C D → a **second**.
- C to E: C D E → a **third**.
- C to G: C D E F G → a **fifth**.
- C to C: eight letters → an **octave**.

Count letters, not frets. C to E and C to Eb are both thirds.

steps.title: Interval quality
steps.body:
The **interval quality** pins down the exact size in half steps:

| Interval | Half steps | From C |
|---|---|---|
| minor 2nd (m2) | 1 | Db |
| major 2nd (M2) | 2 | D |
| minor 3rd (m3) | 3 | Eb |
| major 3rd (M3) | 4 | E |
| perfect 4th (P4) | 5 | F |
| tritone (A4 / d5) | 6 | F# / Gb |
| perfect 5th (P5) | 7 | G |
| minor 6th (m6) | 8 | Ab |
| major 6th (M6) | 9 | A |
| minor 7th (m7) | 10 | Bb |
| major 7th (M7) | 11 | B |
| octave (P8) | 12 | C |

From the tonic of a major scale, every scale note is a major or perfect interval: M2, M3, P4, P5, M6, M7, P8. Minor intervals are one half step smaller than major ones.

diagram.caption: Intervals above C in the C major scale.

steps.title: Intervals on the fretboard
steps.body:
Because strings 6, 5, and 4 are each a perfect 4th apart, intervals form fixed finger patterns there. From a root on string 6 (or string 5, one string higher):

- **M2**: same string, 2 frets up.
- **m3**: next string, 2 frets lower.
- **M3**: next string, 1 fret lower.
- **P4**: next string, same fret.
- **P5**: next string, 2 frets up.
- **M6**: two strings up, 1 fret lower.
- **m7**: two strings up, same fret.
- **P8**: two strings up, 2 frets up.

Crossing onto the B string (string 2) shifts these patterns up one fret, because G to B is a major 3rd instead of a 4th.

steps.title: Intervals above A
steps.caption: A with its M2, M3, P4, P5, M6, and octave, each played after the root.

exercise.prompt: From A on string 6, fret 5, play each interval after the root: M2, M3, P4, P5, P8.

mistakeTips: M3 is on string 5, one fret lower than the root: fret 4.
P4 is straight across: string 5, fret 5. P5 is two frets higher: fret 7.
The octave is two strings up, two frets up: string 4, fret 7.

questions.prompt: C to G is a…
questions.explanation: C D E F G: five letters, seven half steps.

questions.prompt: How many half steps is a minor 3rd?
questions.explanation: Minor 3rd = 3; major 3rd = 4.

questions.prompt: D to F# is a…
questions.explanation: D E F: a third. D to F# is 4 half steps: major.

questions.prompt: What interval is 5 half steps?
questions.explanation: P4 = 5, tritone = 6, P5 = 7.

questions.prompt: E to F is a…
questions.explanation: One half step: minor 2nd.

reviewItems.prompt: Half steps in m3, M3, P4, P5?
On strings 6 to 5, where is the P5 above a root?
What interval is C to A?

lessons.title: Hearing intervals
lessons.summary: Recognize common intervals by ear using public-domain song openings, and play them back.

steps.title: Reference songs
steps.body:
Link each interval to the opening of a song you already know. Sing the song in your head and compare.

| Interval | Rising reference |
|---|---|
| M2 | "Frère Jacques" (first two notes) |
| m3 | "Greensleeves" ("A-las") |
| M3 | "When the Saints" ("Oh when") |
| P4 | "Here Comes the Bride" (Wagner's Bridal Chorus) |
| P5 | "Twinkle, Twinkle" ("Twin-kle, twin-kle") |
| M6 | "My Bonnie Lies Over the Ocean" ("My Bon-") |
| P8 | fret 12 of any string after the open string |

All of these songs are old enough to be in the public domain. If a different song works better for you, use it.

steps.title: Each interval above C
steps.caption: M2, m3, M3, P4, P5, M6, P8, each from C3.

questions.prompt: Listen. Which interval?
questions.explanation: Seven half steps: the "Twinkle, Twinkle" leap.

questions.prompt: Listen. Which interval?
questions.explanation: Four half steps: "Oh when" from "When the Saints".

questions.prompt: Listen. Which interval?
questions.explanation: Five half steps: "Here Comes the Bride".

exercise.prompt: Listen to an interval, then play it back on your guitar starting from A (string 6, fret 5). Intervals come from this lesson's set.

mistakeTips: Sing the second note before you look for it.
Use the reference songs: "Twinkle" for P5, "Here Comes the Bride" for P4.
Use the fretboard patterns from the last lesson once you know the name.

exercise.prompt: Echo: listen to each two-note phrase, then play it back.

mistakeTips: The first note is always C (string 5, fret 3).
P5 from C is G: string 4, fret 5. P4 is F: string 4, fret 3.

lessons.title: Hearing scale degrees
lessons.summary: Hear how each scale degree relates to the tonic, and echo short phrases in C major.

steps.title: Every note has a role
steps.body:
Once a key is set, each scale degree has its own feeling relative to the tonic:

- **1** sounds settled, like home.
- **5** is stable too, but open.
- **3** is stable and gives the major sound.
- **7** leans hard up to 1.
- **4** tends to fall to 3.
- **2** can fall to 1 or rise to 3.
- **6** often falls to 5.

Hearing these tendencies is how musicians work out melodies by ear: they hear "that note wants to go home" and know it is 7 or 2.

steps.title: Tension and release
steps.caption: C major scale up to 7, a pause, then 1. Then 4 falling to 3.

playback.rhythm: q q q q q q h h h h

exercise.prompt: Echo short phrases in C major. Each starts on C (string 5, fret 3).

mistakeTips: Sing it first, then find it.
B2 (degree 7 below the tonic) is on string 6, fret 7, or string 5, fret 2.
Most phrases move by step. Try the neighbor note first.

questions.prompt: Which degree pulls most strongly up to the tonic?
questions.explanation: The leading tone is a half step below 1.

questions.prompt: Which degree sounds most like home?
questions.explanation: The tonic is the point of rest.

reviewItems.prompt: Which scale degree is the leading tone, and where does it want to go?

lessons.title: Scale and interval review
lessons.summary: Review the major scale, scale degrees, and intervals, then play two melodies built from the scale.

steps.title: What you know now
steps.body:
- Major scale: **W W H W W W H**. Half steps between degrees 3–4 and 7–8.
- Degrees: 1 tonic, 2 supertonic, 3 mediant, 4 subdominant, 5 dominant, 6 submediant, 7 leading tone.
- Intervals: m2 1, M2 2, m3 3, M3 4, P4 5, tritone 6, P5 7, m6 8, M6 9, m7 10, M7 11, P8 12 half steps.
- A fingering with no open strings is movable: slide it to change key.

questions.prompt: Spell D major.
choices: D E F G A B C D
D E F# G A B C# D
D E F# G# A B C# D
questions.explanation: D –W– E –W– F# –H– G –W– A –W– B –W– C# –H– D. Two sharps.

questions.prompt: What is the 6th degree of C major?
questions.explanation: C D E F G A.

questions.prompt: G to D is a…
questions.explanation: G A B C D: five letters, 7 half steps.

questions.prompt: Which interval is 9 half steps?
You slide the G major fingering from fret 3 to fret 7 on string 6. What key are you in?
questions.explanation: String 6: G at 3, A at 5, B at 7.

exercise.prompt: Speed check: C major, one octave, open position.

mistakeTips: Even notes matter more than speed.
Keep strict alternate picking.

steps.title: Joy to the World: a scale in disguise
steps.body:
The opening of "Joy to the World" (words by Isaac Watts, 1719; tune published by Lowell Mason, 1839; public domain) is a **D major scale going straight down**: D C# B A G F# E D.

In open position: D (2 fret 3), C# (2 fret 2), B (2 open), A (3 fret 2), G (3 open), F# (4 fret 4), E (4 fret 2), D (4 open).

steps.title: Joy to the World, opening (Mason)
steps.caption: Degrees 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1.
steps.rhythm: h q. e h. q h h h. qr

steps.title: Ode to Joy in G (Beethoven)
steps.caption: The same melody as Stage 1, now in G on strings 3 and 2: G (3 open), A (3 fret 2), B (2 open), C (2 fret 1), D (2 fret 3). It uses only degrees 1 to 5.
steps.rhythm: q q q q q q q q q q q q q. e h q q q q q q q q q q q q q. e h

reviewItems.answer: D E F# G A B C# D
